extracted.intended_audience: scientists, anthropologists, policymakers, public servants, and medical professionals interested in heredity, population policy, and methods for assessing family-line quality (19th-century eugenic proposals)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and proposed criteria for identifying, measuring, and promoting 'superior' hereditary stock (family merit) — including proposed indicators to be used in selection (e.g., competitive exams), population-marriage policy effects, instruments such as endowments, and an illustrated method for composite portraiture to extract typical facial characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of early versus late marriages on population composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare fertility and generation length of early-married and late-married groups to predict how earlier marriage among a favoured class will increase its representation over successive generations (illustrated by age-of-mother fertility tables and multi-generation multiplication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical fertility schedules (table: ages 15–34 giving average fertility), smooth to representative ages (e.g., 17,22,27,32) and compute relative fertility ratios. Account also for generation length (example: generations of 27 vs 36 years; least common multiple 108 years used to project multiplicative effects). Use interpolation for intermediate ages. The text warns that small differences in fertility and earlier generation turnover produce large long-term changes in class composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks for family merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign marks to candidates in competitive selection on the basis of family antecedents — i.e., give weight to the ancestral part of merit as well as to present personal qualifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Family merit should be defined and attested by verifiable facts (see next items). The author suggests conducting careful statistical inquiries linking family antecedents of mature public servants to their earlier examination ranks to determine appropriate mark weights. Verification may require confidential local inquiries and corroboration from multiple sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of a 'thriving family' (occupational success)
rubrics_metrics.description: A thriving family may be inferred from the successive occupations of its several male members in the previous generation and of the two grandfathers; these patent facts are attainable and verifiable locally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use successive male occupations as evidence of family prosperity and stability; such occupational continuity is taken as evidence that descendants are likely to perform well in public service. Recommendation: collect and attest these facts locally for use in selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of a 'healthy and long-lived family' (longevity and living relatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define a healthy and long-lived family by ages at death and by the number and ages of living relatives within specified degrees (used to testify to stamina and forecast long-term performance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect patent, verifiable data: ages at death for relatives and counts/ages of living kin. These facts should be attested and used alongside present health measures to forecast future work capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal signs of superiority versus ancestral evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal attributes (energy, brain, morale, health, success) are already recognised in competition, but ancestral (family) evidence should also be used for forecasting future worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat personal merit as evidence of current capability; treat family history as an additional, distinct predictive element about future development. When two youths have equal personal merit, prefer the one from a thriving, long-lived family for long-term appointments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for careful statistical inquiry and verification before assigning family-merit marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Before implementing family-merit scoring, perform statistical investigations of antecedent family histories of those who fail and succeed, and verify returns to learn the proper weight to assign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author foresees no peculiar difficulty but stresses confidential inquiry, verification, and corroboration across sources. Results from different sources should confirm one another before policy adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of endowments and bequests to favour marriage of desirable stock
rubrics_metrics.description: Local endowments, bequests, or adoptions could be directed to persons showing evidences of high race and belonging to prolific, thriving families to encourage early marriage among the favoured classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical precedent exists for portions to girls and other bequests. Endowments might be structured to promote early marriage among those of high family merit, thereby increasing their reproductive success. Forms are not prescribed, but the text argues such instruments would likely be developed if the value of 'good race' were widely recognized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional law/statute reform to increase reproduction among gifted (repeal celibacy restrictions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reform statutes (e.g., college fellowships forbidding marriage) that have the practical effect of preventing highly endowed persons from procreating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example cited: recent relaxation of statutes at Oxford/Cambridge leading to more marriages; analogous reforms would increase the number of individuals endowed with high scholastic faculties being able to reproduce. Policy implication: identify institutional barriers to early marriage/reproduction and reform them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public recognition and selection processes to incorporate ancestral value
rubrics_metrics.description: Give public recognition in early life to the probability of future performance based on ancestors' past performance; allow family merit to count, even slightly, in competitive examinations to signal the value of ancestry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporating family merit in selection would incentivise collecting family histories and encourage marriage alliances within high-stock families. This recognition is expected to have broad social effects (e.g., charity distribution, social prestige) that favour early marriage among the best-adapted races.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against Malthusian prudential delay in marriage as a policy tool
rubrics_metrics.description: The Malthusian check recommending prudential delay in marriage would be limited to the prudent and self-denying and produce adverse selection: desirable races would leave fewer descendants while undesirable ones would multiply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy must consider differential uptake across classes; delaying marriage as a universal recommendation risks deteriorating the 'race' by selective fertility. The author argues this would have only temporary relief and long-term racial deterioration. Consider alternative checks and the role of social forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of non-misery causes of population decay (apathy, discouragement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Population decline in some groups can be due to listlessness and discouragement (making persons unattractive or unresponsive in forming unions), not solely to 'misery' (inadequate food/war/disease).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy diagnoses should distinguish causes like social apathy and moral discouragement from material misery; remedies differ (e.g., social encouragement vs economic relief). Examples: Jesuit tyranny in parts of South America reducing vivacity and fertility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of charitable distribution to favour best-adapted races
rubrics_metrics.description: Because charity is limited, its distribution should be directed so as to favour families most likely to produce healthy, moral, and intelligent citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author suggests redirecting existing charitable streams (endowments, support) to promote the reproductive success of 'best-adapted' families; this is presented as a mechanism to expedite favorable evolutionary change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouragement of voluntary celibacy among those judged less fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals whose issue would 'probably be less fitted' could be urged to live celibate lives as a public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is proposed as a virtue: few would deserve better of their country than those who choose celibacy from a belief their progeny would be less fit. The recommendation is moral persuasion rather than coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite portraiture: superimpose multiple images to extract typical characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce composite portraits by obtaining drawings or photographs of several similar persons, reducing to the same scale, tracing on transparent paper, and superimposing to obtain an aggregate 'typical' figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: collect multiple likenesses 'alike in most respects, but differing in minor details'; reduce to a common scale; trace on separate transparent sheets; secure them together and view against the light or optically superimpose. This yields extracted typical characteristics of the group. The method originated from the author's suggestion and Herbert Spencer's conversational refinement; several published memoirs are cited as demonstrating successive stages of the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite portraiture as a method for extracting 'typical' group traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the resultant aggregated figure from composite portraiture as a way to identify typical facial/structural features of a group and thus aid anthropological classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composite portraits are intended to reveal aggregate, typical features that might not be obvious from individual variability. Collect sufficiently many subjects and ensure similarity of the sample to avoid spurious results; use optical aggregation rather than inspection of single specimens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call for systematic collection of life-histories (medical and family) as essential data
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical practitioners and others should keep life-histories to improve knowledge of hereditary tendencies, disease theory, and more appropriate patient care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Life-histories provide the materials required for rigorous hereditary study; the medical profession is urged both to keep such records for individual patient benefit and to advocate collective investigation of disease. References to addresses by Sir William Gull and Sir James Paget are given as support.
